vt3_deal_1929.topic: What Mussolini's Italy and the Holy See each got from the Lateran Pacts of 11 February 1929; the 1931 Catholic Action crisis

claims.text: Lateran Treaty Art. 1: Italy reaffirmed the principle of the 1848 Statuto that 'la religione cattolica, apostolica e romana è la sola religione dello Stato'.
Treaty Art. 3: Italy recognized the Holy See's 'piena proprietà e la esclusiva ed assoluta potestà e giurisdizione sovrana sul Vaticano', creating Vatican City.

Treaty Arts. 13-16: the patriarchal basilicas of St John Lateran, St Mary Major and St Paul (Art. 13), the papal palace and Villa Barberini at Castel Gandolfo (Art. 14) and listed properties of curial offices and pontifical institutes (Gregorian, Biblical Institute) received immunities and exemption from expropriation and taxes (Arts. 15-16).
Treaty Art. 24: the Holy See 'vuole rimanere e rimarrà estranea alle competizioni temporali fra gli altri Stati'; Vatican City to be considered neutral territory.
Treaty Art. 26: the Holy See recognized 'il Regno d'Italia sotto la dinastia di Casa Savoia con Roma capitale' and declared the Roman Question definitively and irrevocably closed.
Concordat Art. 1: the government undertook to prevent in Rome anything contrary to the 'carattere sacro della Città Eterna'.

Concordat Art. 19: the Holy See chose bishops but communicated the name to the government to ensure it had no political objections; Art. 20: bishops swore before the Head of State 'fedeltà allo Stato italiano'.
Concordat Art. 30: the State would continue to supplement inadequate incomes of ecclesiastical benefices (the congrua).

Concordat Art. 34: Italy recognized civil effects for the sacrament of marriage governed by canon law; Art. 36: Italy considered 'fondamento e coronamento dell'istruzione pubblica l'insegnamento della dottrina cristiana', extending religious teaching to secondary schools.
Concordat Art. 43: the State recognized Catholic Action organizations; the Holy See renewed for Italian clergy and religious 'il divieto di iscriversi e militare in qualsiasi partito politico'.
Financial Convention Art. 1: Italy paid 750,000,000 lire in cash plus 5% consolidated state bonds of nominal value 1 billion lire, delivered at the exchange of ratifications.

Pius XI, 13 February 1929, said that perhaps 'un uomo come quello che la Provvidenza Ci ha fatto incontrare' was needed, and that with the Concordat he believed he had 'ridato Dio all'Italia e l'Italia a Dio'; the passage does not name Mussolini.

The regime dissolved all Catholic Action youth circles on 30 May 1931 after a campaign begun 19 March 1931; an agreement settling the crisis was signed 2 September 1931; repression of individual members continued until 1943.

In Non abbiamo bisogno (29 June 1931) Pius XI protested the dissolution of Catholic Action youth and university associations, said the regime sought to 'monopolize completely the young', called its ideology 'a real pagan worship of the State' ('Statolatry'), declared the Fascist oath 'as it stands, is unlawful', and said 'We have not said that We wished to condemn the [Fascist] party as such.'

Friedländer (reviewing Kertzer): the Lateran Accords were 'advantageous for both sides'; Mussolini could 'rely on the Holy See's support of his regime and his policies'; Kertzer's thesis that Pius XI and Mussolini needed each other.

vt3_revision_1984.topic: The 1948 Constitution Art. 7, the Villa Madama Agreement of 18 February 1984 and Law 222 of 1985

claims.text: Italian Constitution Art. 7: State and Catholic Church are each in its own order 'indipendenti e sovrani'; relations are regulated by the Lateran Pacts; changes accepted by both parties need no constitutional revision.
Law 121 of 25 March 1985 ratified the Agreement with Additional Protocol signed in Rome on 18 February 1984 by Cardinal Agostino Casaroli for the Holy See and Bettino Craxi for the Italian Republic.

Agreement Art. 1: State and Church each in its own order 'indipendenti e sovrani'; Art. 2.4 the Republic recognizes Rome's particular significance as the pope's see; Art. 3 Church authorities freely appoint and notify civil authorities of appointments of diocesan bishops; no oath provision.

Agreement Art. 7.6: a joint commission (Commissione paritetica) to draft norms on ecclesiastical entities and property; Art. 8.1: canonical marriages have civil effects if transcribed in civil registers; Art. 9.2: Catholic teaching continues in state schools with the 'diritto di scegliere se avvalersi o non avvalersi'.
Additional Protocol point 1: 'Si considera non più in vigore il principio, originariamente richiamato dai Patti lateranensi, della religione cattolica come sola religione dello Stato italiano.'

Craxi became prime minister on 4 August 1983; on 28 January 1984 the Chamber of Deputies authorized him to conclude the agreement by 338 to 67 with 30 abstentions; the reform ended the state religion, the bishops' oath, direct state pay of priests (replaced by otto per mille) and compulsory religious instruction.

Law 222/1985 set up diocesan institutes for clergy support and a central institute set up by the CEI (Art. 21); institutes provide 'il congruo e dignitoso sostentamento del clero' at levels set by the CEI (Art. 24); deductible gifts to the central institute up to 2 million lire from 1989 (Art. 46); from tax year 1990 'una quota pari all'otto per mille dell'imposta sul reddito delle persone fisiche' is allocated (Art. 47); unexpressed choices distributed 'in proporzione alle scelte espresse'; Art. 48 purposes (State: world hunger, natural disasters etc.; Church: worship needs, clergy support, charity); Art. 49 joint commission reviews every three years; Art. 50 transitional payments to the CEI 1987-1989.

ICSC 2024: 31,053 priests in the support system; €389,000,000 from otto per mille allocated by CEI; €7,969,855 in deductible donations; full-time priest monthly pay €1,049.60 to €1,981.12 (12 payments), bishops €2,204.16; 28,150 received an integration, 459 full remuneration, 2,444 none needed.

vt3_eight_per_mille.topic: Otto per mille: mechanism, latest figures, CEI allocation 2026, Corte dei conti critique

claims.text: CEI 2026 allocation: total €1,086,752,778.01 (advance for 2026 €1,063,069,466.83 plus €23,683,311.18 adjustment on 2023); worship and pastoral €408,208,000 (dioceses €158m; church building €104m; cultural heritage €25m; catechesis €58m; regional ecclesiastical tribunals €13m; national needs €50.208m); charity €284,544,000 (dioceses €150m; development of peoples (abroad) €80m; national €54.544m); clergy support €394,000,000.

MEF data (tax year 2022, paid 2026): about €1.6bn distributed; of about 42m taxpayers just over 16.8m (about 40.1%) made a valid choice; Catholic Church 11.35m choices, about €1.06bn, 67.3-67.8%; State 4.53m choices, €426m, 26.6-26.8%; Waldensians €46.4m; Italian Buddhist Union €17.4m; Soka Gakkai €8.5m; Union of Italian Jewish Communities €4.5m; Orthodox Archdiocese €3.68m; Hindu Union €2.41m; Adventists €1.86m; Assemblies of God €1.58m.

MEF data (tax year 2021, paid 2025): 41,497,318 taxpayers; 16,687,453 (40.21%) made a valid choice; Catholic Church 11,599,375 choices (69.51% of choices; 68.72% of the amount); State 24.63% of choices, 25.45% of amount. Tax year 2020: Church 71.00% of the amount.

Corte dei conti (control section, 2015, as reported by Avvenire) objected that citizens are involved 'indipendentemente dalla propria volontà' through distribution of unexpressed choices, criticized the State's 'scarso interesse' in its own quota and the churches' heavy advertising; the CEI replied that the system is 'un caso di democrazia nell'indirizzo della spesa pubblica', comparing unexpressed choices to non-voters in elections, and that accounts are published annually.
